https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6ly: Negotiations at the COP31 UN climate summit in Turkey are in deadlock and have been suspended for the night, after running more than a day over time, as countries have been unable to agree on a new global climate deal.
The EU and Pacific island nations are amongst a group pushing back against the latest draft agreement which included no reference to reducing the world's demand for fossil fuels.
A second sticking point involves a push from the Africa Group to get commitments on more money for adaptation - but the EU has previously said it would not support this.
Negotiating teams due to fly out on Sunday morning are now moving their flights to Monday in a sign that a deal is not yet in sight.
If countries cannot reach consensus - which is required by the UN's climate talks process - the negotiations could be suspended.
In that case the summit would end with no deal and be reconvened next year. This has only happened once before since countries started holding COP climate meetings in 1995.
Panama's Environment Minister is pushing for language on fossil fuels to be in the final agreement
On Saturday, EU Commissioner for Climate Wopke Hoekstra said if the bloc could not get "what is needed in terms of climate action... then there's no deal."
The UK's chief negotiator, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, remained more hopeful and said her team was still working to get an agreement.

"These are difficult negotiations, but discussions remain productive and there is a deal to be done. The UK is pushing hard for an outcome and we will keep working in the coming hours to bring countries together."
Another risk is that negotiating teams have to start journeys home, and the meeting could lose the critical number of nations needed to pass any global agreement.
More climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledged

Ministers from Panama, Solomon Islands, Cote d'Ivoire and the EU are fighting to get a commitment to move away from oil, gas and coal back into the final agreement after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi Arabia pushed for its removal.

"It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels and we simply will not put up with it," said Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama's minister for the environment.
His words were echoed by France's Minister of Ecological Transition, Monique Barbut.

She took aim at several references in the text to carbon capture, use and storage - the technology that takes emissions when they are released and stores them underground - as a licence for other countries to keep burning oil and gas.
"We cannot be announcing to the world that we are now getting to 1.5 increase in the temperature and do business like nothing was happening," Barbut said.
For the first time at a COP the agreement - known officially as the Antalya Accords - could acknowledge that the goal of keeping global temperature rise below 1.5C has been missed.
Beyond this point scientists warn , external that millions more people will be exposed to sea level rise and extreme heat.
But Chris Bowen, Australia's climate change and energy minister who is leading negotiations, pushed back on the need to include language on fossil fuels.
He argued that this summit was about implementation, and should focus on the move towards clean energy sources.

Away from COP, renewable energy is growing at unprecedented rates. For the first time this year a modern renewable source - solar panels - was the biggest contributor to meeting new global energy demand , outstripping oil and gas , external .

The International Energy Agency also warned this week that the longer disruption to fuel supplies through the Strait of Hormuz due to the Iran War continues, the stronger the incentive to switch to electricity powered by renewables.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq4g: Flames engulfed Hudson Valley farm as 200 first responders arrived at the scene
A fire broke out at one of the largest foie gras farms in the US on Thursday, killing an undetermined number of birds.
The blaze engulfed several barns at Hudson Valley Farms in upstate New York before firefighters could get inside. No information has been provided as to what caused the fire.
Crews managed to rescue hundreds of young birds and hatchlings, and no workers or first responders were injured, according to local news outlets.

Foie gras, made from the fattened liver of a duck or goose, has long drawn protests from animal rights groups because the birds are force-fed. Voters in both Washington DC and Denver backed bans on foie gras sales in this month's midterm elections.
Hudson Valley Farms is in a legal battle with the state of New York over its foie gras ban
Marcus Henley, manager of Hudson Valley Foie Gras in Ferndale, New York, told local news outlet Radio Catskill that the fire destroyed two buildings housing ducks and geese.
"The building isn't there anymore," Henley said, adding that he suspected an electrical malfunction may have started the blaze, although this has not been confirmed.
The company does not disclose how many birds it hosts at one time. Commercial poultry farms can typically house thousands of birds.
Westchester News 12 reported that the emergency response to the fire in the early hours of Thursday morning involved 37 fire departments and 200 first responders.
The fire spread rapidly, and the metal-clad, wood-frame structure of the building made it difficult for firefighters to stop the flames from spreading inside the barn.
Hudson Valley Foie Gras and the local fire department did not respond to a request for comment.

Foie gras producers have long been criticised by animal rights groups due to the production process, which involves the force feeding of birds through plastic tubes, which allows them to gain over a third of their body weight in a short period of time.
New York moved to ban the product in 2019, and Hudson Valley farms have been in litigation with the state since.
At a city council hearing in 2019, Henley argued against the ban, saying that journalists who visited the farm found "nothing inhumane" about their practices.

Animal rights activist group PETA told the BBC that they will erect a billboard nearby in memory of the birds who perished, and encouraged Hudson Valley farms to donate surviving birds to local sanctuaries.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8xg: Switching to heat pumps is seen as a key way to help meet the UK's net zero targets
Developers will have to install heat pumps and solar panels in all new homes in England under regulations announced in March .
The changes are estimated to add £10,000 to the price of new homes, though owners will likely save money on energy bills over the long term.
In January, the government introduced a £15bn Warm Homes Plan to help UK households pay for green technologies as part of efforts to reduce fossil fuel use and energy bills.
But the autumn budget cut £1bn from the programme to pay for defence.
Heating homes accounts for about a fifth of the UK's planet-warming emissions, so switching from gas and oil to heat pumps is seen as a key way to help meet net zero targets .
Heat pumps run on electricity instead of gas and are more efficient than traditional boilers. They warm buildings by absorbing and amplifying heat from the air, ground or water.

Air source heat pumps - the most common type - suck in outdoor air and pass it over tubes containing refrigerant fluids. The heat from the outdoor air causes the refrigerants to evaporate into a gas. Compressing the gas increases the temperature, and this heat is passed around the home.
The system consists of a box measuring about 1m x 1m x 0.4m (3ft x 3ft x 1.3ft) which stands outside the property, as well as a heat pump unit and hot water cylinder inside the property.
The indoor unit is about the size of a gas boiler, while the size of the cylinder depends on the property.
Ground source heat pumps are more efficient than air source models.
However, they are typically more expensive and less commonly used, as they require either a deep bore hole or a large horizontal system dug into the ground.
The Boiler Upgrade Scheme provides a grant of £7,500 towards the cost of an air source or ground source heat pump for homeowners in England and Wales.
Households typically spend an additional £5,000 on top of the grant, which the UK's spending watchdog warned is too high for many .

The grant can be used for existing homes and non-domestic buildings. The property must have an eligible Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) - a measure of how your property is performing - issued in the last 10 years.
Properties no longer need to have existing loft or cavity wall insulation to qualify for the grant, which can save around £2,500 in upfront costs.
Check if you are eligible for the Boiler Upgrade Scheme , external
For low-income households and those in social housing, the government is providing an extra £5bn for the Warm Homes Local Grant , external and the Social Housing Fund , external .
Scotland , external and Northern Ireland , external have separate schemes to help make homes more efficient.
UK households can also apply for low and no interest loans of between £7,500 and £35,000 to install green technologies under the Warm Homes Loan Scheme , external .
The government has promised to keep funding for the Boiler Upgrade Scheme at £400m in 2027-28 before increasing it in line with inflation.
However, this represents a significant cut compared to what was previously announced.

Some of the money the energy and environment departments have to spend on loans and investments is also being diverted towards the £4.7bn "Your First Home" scheme, which aims to help people purchase a property.
This could mean further cuts to the Warm Homes Scheme, but the government has said it "remains committed to heat-pump deployment".
Heat pump installations currently benefit from a 0% VAT rate, but this is set to rise to 5% in April 2027.

While the upfront costs remain substantial, heat pumps could become cheaper to run than gas boilers, according to the Climate Change Committee (CCC) , external , which advises the UK government on cutting emissions.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr78: Buttermere has been described as a "fragile ecosystem under pressure"
Tourism, infrastructure challenges and "outdated, undersized and poorly maintained" wastewater systems are contributing to the ecological decline of a popular lake, an environmental group has warned.
Buttermere, in the Lake District, has seen rising nutrient levels in recent years which can lead to excess phosphorus and blankets of algae.
A new report has found farming practices alone "cannot account" for the changes.
West Cumbria Rivers Trust (WCRT), a charity which tracked down the sources of phosphorus for the study, argues "urgent regulatory action and maintenance guidance are needed".
The Buttermere Nutrient Investigations Project was commissioned and funded by the Environment Agency (EA) after the lake was last year found to be failing to meet total phosphorus targets.
WCRT said the investigation showed Buttermere - a designated Site of Special Scientific Interest and Special Area of Conservation - was a "fragile ecosystem under pressure".
Buttermere is a naturally nutrient-poor lake, the organisation said, which provides a welcoming environment for sensitive species, such as the Arctic charr cold-water fish.
But algae triggered by excess phosphorus can "choke out these rare habitats and degrade the lake's protected status", WCRT added.

Local wastewater infrastructure was identified as a "key area of concern", the organisation said, while agricultural investigations across major landholdings found no evidence of systemic diffuse pollution or excessive nutrient use, with soil management plans broadly appropriate.
As they are not connected to mains drainage, many properties in the area rely on septic tanks or package treatment plants.

However, WCRT said a number of the 11 septic tank systems identified in the catchment were "undersized, poorly maintained or past their effective lifespan, with several suspected to be discharging directly to surface water, which is not compliant with the regulations".
Although most owners were keen to help the environment, the trust said there was a "widespread lack of awareness" about how the private systems worked and what level of maintenance was needed.
Surveys also revealed just over 40% of visitors had dogs with them and many were walked along sensitive lakeshore paths.
Nutrient fertilisation by the animals "could be significant", it was found.

WCRT CEO Jodie Mills, said: "Our investigations show that water quality in Buttermere is suffering primarily due to private wastewater systems that are undersized, poorly maintained or overwhelmed during peak seasonal surges.
"Many home and business owners simply didn't realise their tanks weren't performing properly.
"This creates a hidden source of pollution, and urgent regulatory action and maintenance guidance are needed to protect this special lake."

In addition to calling for regulation and enforcement, the trust said it would be providing wastewater guidance for homeowners on its website and engaging with the local parish council and the Lake District Visitor Management Group, which includes the National Trust and the Lake District National Park Authority.
Responsibility for the regulation of discharges belongs to the EA.
Peter Miles, the organisation's nature, monitoring and technical manager, said the report provided "valuable information about the sources of excess nutrients" in Buttermere.

He added: "Sources of pollution are often very complex and we urge everyone living or working in Buttermere, and those visiting, to play their part in reducing the amount of pollution entering the lake, from checking their private sewage systems to clearing up after their dogs."

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/pacific/27705: Scientists exploring the Mariana Trench in the western Pacific have discovered evidence of the world's deepest known explosive volcanic eruptions, challenging conventional understanding of volcanic activity beneath the ocean.
New Scientist reports that a robotic submarine found evidence of explosive eruptions more than 6,100 metres below sea level near the Challenger Deep, southwest of Guam.
The findings were published on 23 November in the scientific journal Frontiers in Earth Science.
Researchers exploring the trench in late 2024 had originally set out to investigate why the Challenger Deep, the world's deepest known point at nearly 11 kilometres below sea level, was so deep.
Instead, they stumbled upon volcanic rock deposits formed by explosive eruptions at depths where immense water pressure was thought to inhibit such activity.
"Explosive volcanism near trenches is unusual, so we were very surprised," lead researcher Robert J Stern of the University of Texas at Dallas said in a statement released by the journal.
"These are the deepest pyroclastic rocks documented to date from anywhere in the ocean."
The researchers conducted seven dives along a roughly 300-kilometre stretch of the southern Mariana Trench using a remotely operated vehicle.
The study also suggests that geological changes beneath the trench could influence the movement of tectonic plates across the western Pacific.
Scientists hope to return to explore greater depths and pinpoint where the volcanic eruptions originated.
The Mariana Trench began forming about 52 million years ago when the Pacific tectonic plate started sliding beneath the Philippine Sea plate.

Lifesaving flotation buoys on a Far North beach have disappeared twice in recent weeks, even as one was used in a rescue further south at McLeod Bay.
The buoys were the brainchild of Pat Millar after Wairongoa 'Magoo' Renata drowned at Little Cable Bay in 2018 while attempting to save children caught in a rip.
Millar originally founded Operation Flotation, a charitable trust that installs the devices at beaches]. She now volunteers at Surf Life Saving New Zealand as its public rescue equipment officer.
Equipment went missing from Taipā Beach in early October, NZME reported, and replacement gear was presumably stolen again in early November.
"I don't know what's going on in people's minds because I just can't comprehend," Millar told RNZ's Nine to Noon on Wednesday.
"But I'm assuming, I'm hoping that if they're taking them, that they're going to use them for the purpose that they were designed, you know? To float when you're out at sea.
"But I have decided that I'm not really going to focus too much negative energy on that and that just carry on. There's not much I can do about it."
The next generation of flotation devices might have trackers, she said, but that would add "a whole new realm of expense".
"It's something that we're always talking about and always, if we come up with an idea, for certain it'll happen."
She said if people needed flotation devices, or thought they were better used in a different spot, to just ask her.
"It's a community effort, it really is a community effort. It's not just me."
Millar got the idea to bring flotation buoys to New Zealand after seeing how they saved lives in Hawaii. Within two years, she had 20 set up at beaches around the upper North Island.
But water safety organisations told her she shouldn't be encouraging people to attempt rescues if they weren't trained in lifesaving techniques.
"My response is always, 'But if it's a dad or if it's a mum, they're getting in.' So if they're going to get in anyway, we should really give them something to help with that rescue."
By 2021, she had Surf Life Saving New Zealand on side, who helped write up some standards for the equipment.

"I couldn't believe it, I was so happy. And so those standards were actually published at the end of 2023, and they set out the signage, they actually changed the device from a rescue tube, which actually deteriorated quite quickly in the sun, to a rescue buoy. So it's a hard plastic rescue buoy."
Accident Compensation Corporation then got involved, providing funding to expand coverage, and there are now 170 of them around the country.
In the event of an emergency, Millar said the most important thing was to call 111 first "so you know you've got help coming behind you".
"The next thing is if you can't really swim then don't try. Just watch and look, so that when someone who is prepared to go in the water arrives, you know where the person is."
Once you are in the water, it's important not to get too close to the person struggling as they might pull you under, she said.
"So you get to within two metres of them, you pull the buoy towards you and hand it to them and just say, 'Here, hold on to this.'"

That is the question being asked by Vaovasatoa Albert Scott, along with others in South Auckland in reaction to Auckland Council's proposed budget plans under its Fairer Funding model, which would see drastic cuts to a range of cherished services and community facilities.

And it is those living in predominantly low income, Pacific communities like Māngere and Ōtara that will be hit particularly hard, with reduced maintence services of parks, shorter library hours along with increased charges to use swimming pools being proposed in Auckland Council's consultation document for its 2026/2027 annual plan .

The document also revealed that both the Māngere-Ōtāhuhu Local Board and Ōtara-Papatoetoe Local Board areas will potentially be hit with a targeted rate of between $27 and $47 per household to help raise around $1million each to fund existing services.
In response to the budget plan, one South Auckland politician, who did not wish to be named, has admitted the cuts required are so severe that certain facilities may need to be closed altogether.
"The easiest way to make up the shortfall is to just close a library or community centre," they said.
Vaovasatoa Albert Scott, centre, with his team at a community event in Māngere.
But for Vaovasatoa, who helps run a range of events in Māngere as part his business Haddon House, such a step would impact the very fabric of his community.
"These facilities on paper might look just another dollar on a budget sheet, but these facilities, are a reflection of our community and our culture.
"It's where we celebrate language weeks, different cultural events, or you know, have women's weaving classes or arts exhibitions."
Lotu Fuli says Ōtara Pools are too shallow for manus, citing safety concerns.
"These are things some people might think of as nice to have or luxury items," Fuli said.
"But to us who live here and especially to communities like ours here in Manukau, these are essential services that help our families and so it's about what's important to the soul of our city."

Vaovasatoa has also run workshops at local libraries, upskilling locals on how to manage their money. He added that cuts at a time when so many are struggling with the cost of living is particularly galling.
"Long gone are the days where you just go to a library to read a book," he said.
"We've got people doing their CVs there. It's where people go for their council queries, you've got kids in there with their afterschool programs. It's buzzing.

"And so when you start to reduce those hours or take their facilities away. You're taking away another place where our youth can go and play and be active, and obviously they can stay out of trouble as well."
Vaovasatoa Albert Scott, a South Auckland community advocate and businessman
Fuli explained that it is council's new way of funding local boards that has resulted in the change - described as the Fairer Funding model .

"These two local boards are looking at a shortfall of about a million dollars or more dollars, and so they have to make those very difficult decisions around what that money goes towards, and what needs to be cut in order to meet those shortfalls."
But she added that one way to stop further cuts will be for the council to hear from the public about why these services canot be reduced.
"These kinds of services are what I believe and many residents believe, are core to our soul as a city, but not everyone around the governing body would think the same.

Australian employers are still paying a premium over New Zealand - but the gap might not be as large as you think in some cases.
Recruiter Robert Walters has released its latest salary guide, which shows what a number of corporate roles across finance and tech are paying on both sides of the Tasman.
An Auckland finance manager is earning an average NZ$160,000 a year according to the survey, while the equivalent in New South Wales earns A$165,000, or about NZ$200,000.
Financial controllers were getting an average NZ$210,000 in Auckland, or NZ$300,000 in New South Wales.
Some tech roles were more similar. An Auckland cloud engineer was earning NZ$160,000 according to the guide, compared to NZ$170,000 in Australia.
Data scientists were getting NZ$150,000 in Auckland and NZ$210,000 in Victoria. AI engineers also earned more in Australia.
The report showed some differences within New Zealand, too. A tax account was earning an average $135,000 in Auckland, $120,000 in Wellington and $115,000 in Christchurch.
A graduate accountant was getting $72,500 in Auckland, and $67,500 in Wellington and Christchurch.

Robert Walters associate director Alyse Young said Australian employers were still generally paying more. "They're a much bigger country with different state organisations … there are a lot of different factors, versus New Zealand we're a lot smaller."
She said Australia's superannuation scheme, in which employers made a 12 percent contribution on top of employees' salary also made their remuneration more generous.

"I think a lot of organisations in New Zealand haven't necessarily moved or increased their salaries over time as much as potentially Australia has, which has also created a sort of bigger divide over time as well."

She said wage growth had slowed here although not as much as some people might have thought. "We're still seeing people get small increases in organisations but we're also seeing a greater shift of people moving roles to look for that salary increase . Where people might have stayed in roles for five to 10 years a period of time ago, their tenure in roles is shorter. A lot of the time that is partly to do with salary factors and development as well."

Robert Walters' surveying showed almost 80 percent of employees said their pay was not fully keeping pace with the cost of living. More than half were thinking about changing jobs in the next year, usually for better salary or benefits.
"People feel like their income isn't increasing at the same rate.

"But I also think different things that we're seeing people start to value , maybe not quite as much as pay, but the flexibility and those sorts of things as well, we are seeing people sort of favour a little bit more than just salary increases."
More than 60 percent said they would consider leaving work or would leave if their flexibility was removed. Almost 90 percent said AI helped their work.

Young said a couple of years ago there had been a large spike in migration to Australia. "People talking about their families moving overseas and relocating kids who are in school and all those sorts of things. I think that's definitely slowed down.

"We're still seeing a lot of the grads or people who are in the first five years of their working careers making the move over there. But we are seeing the more mature workforce that we deal with a lot in our role staying put. And there's opportunities around for them more so than maybe there was a couple of years ago. I think that's also a positive thing in terms of keeping some of those skilled professionals around as well."

It may have been worth staying up late, or setting an early alarm, to catch a glimpse of the moon overnight.
November's full moon reached 'peak illumination' a few hours ago, and this one is a supermoon - meaning it coincides with the moon being at its closest point to Earth in its orbit.
The beaver reference is a nod to the time of year in North America when the industrious dam-building mammals prepare for winter.
It's the first of three consecutive supermoons with another due next month.

November's full moon appeared about 17 percent larger and 30 percent brighter than the smallest full moon of the year, Noah Petro, chief of NASA's Planetary Geology, Geophysics and Geochemistry Lab at Goddard Space Flight Centre in Maryland told CNN .
The Beaver Supermoon setting over the Molfetta skyline near the Passari Tower in Molfetta, Italy, on November 24, 2026.
Josh Aoraki, astronomy teacher at Te Wānanga o Aotearoa, told Morning Report two to four supermoons occurred each year.
Each supermoon involves the two extreme points of the moon, which has an elliptical path rather than circular.
"If it happens to be a full moon near its closest point [to Earth] it's slightly bigger, slightly brighter in the sky, hence a supermoon."
Its scientific name is a perigee whereas the term supermoon has come from astrology, Aoraki said.
Even if it was cloudy or hazy, the full moon looked extra stunning and was often offset by beautiful skies, he said.
If people missed it on Tuesday night it might be even better on Wednesday because it would be rising about an hour after sunset.
"It takes on that really beautiful orange hue which is really spectacular. It stops people in their tracks, and 'oh my God, look at the moon'."
Aoraki said he was now teaching Māori astronomy as part of a new adult education course.
It was one of the first in the country and integrated the sky and land in a more holistic way than the Gregorian calendar which is more commonly used.
A man fishes from a jetty as the Beaver supermoon rises over the coastline of Kuwait City.
December's full moon, the last of 2026, will also be the year's biggest and brightest supermoon, according to The Old Farmer's Almanac .
Known as the cold moon, it will reach peak illumination on 23 December. The first full moon of 2027, also a supermoon and called the Wolf Moon, will follow on 22 January.

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/environment/2: Link: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/environment/2769719%2Fhow-the-pohutukawa-went-global
Nothing signals a Kiwi summer quite like red stamens scattered across the bonnet of a seemingly abandoned car just up the road.
Pōhutukawa have started to bloom. But as iconic as they are, it's easy to take Aotearoa's Christmas trees for granted.
One man who would never do that is University of Auckland Associate Professor of Biological Sciences Bruce Burns.
He told RNZ's First Up there are more varieties of pōhutukawa than many New Zealanders might realise.
"There's at least 42 different cultivars that are produced around the country for planting in gardens and so on.
"Of course there's the main wild pōhutukawa but as well as that, we have a number of species of pōhutukawa that we have planted within New Zealand that come from different parts of the Pacific."

"We have a Tahitian pōhutukawa which is quite common in gardens around Auckland, which is Metrosideros collina, a different species, and we also have a species from the Kermadec Islands, Metrosideros kermadecensis, and that's slightly different from our wild pōhutukawa."
While pōhutukawa are now a familiar sight around much of New Zealand's coastline, their natural range is much smaller.
Burns says the native pōhutukawa is originally a North Island tree.
"In terms of distribution, the natural range of our wild pōhutukawa only really goes down to a line from about Gisborne to Taranaki, so going south, anything in the South Island has been planted.
"But of course if you go down to Wellington, we have a lot of planted pōhutukawa people have brought to Wellington and they've naturalised."
A view of a beach on Waiheke Island, framed by pōhutukawa flowers.
The trees have also established themselves along parts of the South Island coastline, having originally been brought there by people.

"It does also grow down the South Island around the coast and that has also been brought to that area by humans. So in terms of the genetics, they will have been derived from the North Island pōhutukawa originally."
And while the pōhutukawa is famous for its vibrant red flowers, not every tree puts on the same display.

"There is a very beautiful golden or yellow pōhutukawa that was discovered on Motiti Island in about 1940, a sort of genetic mutant, if you like, and that's been planted in various places around the country as well.
"There's a yellow variety but there is also, occasionally, very occasionally, you'll get a white pōhutukawa or even a pink pōhutukawa."
And if you're lucky, you might spot pink-flowering pōhutukawa around Rotorua.

"Unusually, there are some wild pōhutukawa growing inland around the Rotorua lakes and they're known for having a sort of very pinky-coloured flower rather than the vibrant red that we're so used to."
The flowering season stretches from late November to early February, but individual trees only bloom for around two weeks .
Burns says the trees stagger their flowering across that period.
"Interestingly, it seems if a pōhutukawa flowers early one year, it will flower early within that window in subsequent years.
"So they don't all flower together, although there is a peak of flowering of course just sort of mid-December coming up to Christmas, which is why we call it our wonderful Christmas tree."
But New Zealand's beloved Christmas tree hasn't stayed within our shores. And in some places overseas, it's become an unwelcome guest.

"We often in New Zealand complain about invasive plant species that have been brought from other countries, but we're not innocent ourselves in contributing to invasive species in other parts of the world, and pōhutukawa is actually one of those."

"Stressed about money and working multiple jobs" - that is how Massey University student Ellice Lawrie describes the new normal in higher education.
She said she had to find work at the student magazine Massive as she struggled to afford the basics .
"[Around] $330 is the max amount of money you can get out as a loan through StudyLink for living costs.
"So I'm living off of that, but my rent's $212. And then once you add utilities and food onto that, it's kind of just enough money to get by, but only just."
Around two-thirds of students worked jobs while studying, up from half in 2021, according to the Ministry of Education's 'Working while Studying' report.
The report found completion rates for those engaging in part-time study were higher than those not working at all but dropped when the intensity of work increased.
Lawrie said she'd struggled to find the right balance - often prioritising her paid work.
"Especially because that's what I'm getting paid for. So it feels a lot more important to be focusing on."
She said she wanted to focus more on her studies, but she was still looking for more work to make ends meet.
"But I'm even thinking, as I'm looking: 'I don't know if I could fit another job on top of what I've got'."
Te ao Māori writer at Massive and soon-to-be graduate Kamaia Bainbridge-Frost said she knew she'd have to work multiple jobs while studying.
She started out as a baby-sitter in her first year. By her last year, she was working for the student magazine and as an independent contractor for different kaupapa.
She estimated she spent 20 hours a week on her paid work and around 40 hours on her studies.
"There's no such thing as a work-life balance when you're a uni student. I think it's just work and surviving."
She said she tried to get out and see friends but she put her degree and future career first.
"The work that I have the privilege of doing and have done in the past is very fulfilling to me and I also work with people that I love, that are some of my closest friends."
But she said this had come at the cost of her mental and physical health.
Victoria University Student Association President Aidan Donoghue (L) and Cam Dickson.
Victoria University of Wellington Student Association president Aidan Donoghue said many students were struggling.

"Not everyone has the same sort of safety nets and many people might be coming out here and really just going all or nothing in a university. There isn't a second option and failure certainly isn't one."
He said the association and the university had been collaborating to provide more support and hardship grants.
"Wellington's been hit extremely hard with the lack of jobs and the competitive nature of just even part-time hospitality or retail work."
Student Job Search's chief executive Louise Saviker said students needed the experience for their future careers.
"Employers love students who have experience in hospitality, retail, for example, no matter what kind of career they're planning on having [because it] teaches them how to work."
She said employers were feeling squeezed and as a result were demanding work-ready graduates who needed less training.

Greenpeace has accused Fonterra of creating the very problem it's trying to fix by asking for consent to dump 22 million litres of excess milk.
And Environment Canterbury has asked Fonterra for more information on its application .
The diary giant had applied to the Canterbury Regional Council to vary, or add to, its existing wastewater consents so it can dispose of surplus milk .
Fonterra's application stated the milk would be incorporated into existing wastewater systems or applied directly to land in the region.

Fonterra director of NZ Manufacturing Chris Kane told Morning Report on Tuesday the company had the capacity to process the milk, and the dumping would only be if there was something major like a power cut or a natural disaster - though there is no mention of a force majeure event in the application to the regional council.
Greenpeace executive director Russel Norman says the law already allows Fonterra to dump milk in the event of an emergency.
"Fonterra lobbied very hard to weaken fresh water standards, it lobbied very hard to make sure that they wouldn't face a price on their climate emissions," he told Morning Report on Wednesday.
"And of course it's lobbied against court cases to make them accountable. All of those things combined with market pressures have resulted in this big surge in dairy conversion."
But while milk production has increased, processing capacity has not, he said.

"This is a problem Fonterra is making, [the] dairy industry more generally. There was a moratorium on new conversions that was in place until 1 January 2025. That was in place in order to give regional councils time to come up with freshwater plans to manage the huge freshwater pollution coming out of the dairy sector.

"Then we get a change of Government, Luxon Government comes in and all the plans are blocked; they pass special legislation to prevent regional councils introducing these new freshwater management plans, but the moratorium comes off."
In a letter to Fonterra, the council requested information on where the milk would be dumped , the impact on the land, and the duration of the dumping.

"The application does not provide sufficient level of detail for CRC science teams nor Te Runanga o Arowhenua to fully understand the proposal in relation to the location of the discharges, the soil types, and the interaction between this discharge and existing discharges," the letter said.
It also outlined mana whenua concerns that milk dumped near the Clandeboye factory site would leach into waterways.

"Mana whenua has expressed concerns that the discharge of raw milk onto a site with a high-water table will result in contaminants leaching into these waterways and impacting mahika kai (traditional food gathering) values."
The deadline for the response from Fonterra was 19 November. RNZ has approached the council for comment.

A Fonterra spokesperson said the company had not had to dispose of milk this season, and that it was already past the peak processing period. It also did not foresee the need to dispose of milk next season.
Norman called on the Government to "step in and reinsert the moratorium on your dairy conversions so that we can actually develop proper fresh water protection".
https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/jordie-ba: All Blacks star Jordie Barrett has been named a finalist for World Rugby’s Player of the Year award, one of rugby’s biggest individual honours.

It caps off a strong year for New Zealand rugby, with two Kiwi players now up for some of the sport’s most prestigious individual prizes.
Fans will have to wait to find out whether Barrett and Lakai can bring the awards home, with winners usually revealed once the busy November international rugby window wraps up.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/giant-new: Northland has its first wind farm, with power company Mercury officially opening the $287 million Kaiwaikawe Wind Farm near Dargaville on Monday.

The wind farm sits at Ōmāmari, on the region’s west coast, on farmland run by Pāmu. Mercury chief executive Stew Hamilton cut the ribbon alongside Kaipara Deputy Mayor Gordon Lambeth and Northland MP Grant McCallum.
“Today we recognise the skill and commitment of everyone who has helped bring Northland’s first wind farm to life,” Hamilton said.

The wind farm has 12 huge turbines, each standing 206 metres tall from the ground to the tip of the blade when it’s pointing straight up. That makes them the tallest turbines in New Zealand, and the second-tallest structures in the whole country, beaten only by Auckland’s Sky Tower.
Together, the turbines can make about 77 megawatts of electricity. That’s enough power for more than 31,000 homes once the wind farm is running at full strength.
Construction began in March last year, and Mercury says the project remains on schedule and on budget, with full power generation expected by 2027.
“We remain on track to complete the Kaiwaikawe development on schedule and on budget,” Hamilton said.
Wind farms like this one help New Zealand make electricity without burning fuels like coal or gas, which is better for the environment and for the climate.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/air-nz-br: Air New Zealand is flying long-haul routes from Christchurch again, after a non-stop flight to Singapore took off on 28 October 2026. Long-haul flights are very long trips, often across oceans. Since 2020, the airline had flown very few of them from Christchurch.
More routes are on the way. Direct flights to Tokyo in Japan start on 28 November, and flights to Perth in Australia start on 30 November. A seasonal service to Bali is planned for winter 2027.

Christchurch Airport is expecting its busiest international summer yet, with 21 percent more international seats than before. That’s roughly one extra seat for every five. Even so, Auckland still handles nearly three times as many passengers.

Will smaller towns benefit? Christchurch is also a hub, or meeting point, for flights to smaller places like Queenstown, Dunedin, Nelson, Hokitika and Invercargill. Ajai Jayathilakan, an aviation lecturer at Massey University, warns that these regional communities could miss out.

Figures from NZ Airports looked at routes where another airline, Jetstar, doesn’t compete with Air NZ. On those routes, fares rose 4.2 percent and seat numbers dropped by the same amount. Billie Moore, who led NZ Airports at the time, said, “Regional New Zealand is living the reality of this every day.”
Jayathilakan says the new flights are good news for the South Island. He says ideas like better-linked flight timetables could help smaller towns share in the benefits.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/famous-ba: One of the Batmobiles from the 1992 film Batman Returns is going up for auction near Los Angeles, in the United States. It could become the most expensive Batmobile ever sold.

Julien’s Auctions expects the car to sell for between US$5 million and US$7 million, which is about NZ$9 million to NZ$12 million. The current record is US$4.6 million (about NZ$8.4 million). It was set in 2013 by the Batmobile Adam West drove in the 1960s Batman TV series.
Three special Batmobiles were built for Batman Returns, which was directed by Tim Burton. Julien’s calls this one the “Number One Hero car”, and it was used in most of the film’s driving scenes.
The glossy black car is about six metres long and has two large tail fins. It still has its original paint, a Chevrolet V-8 engine, and a remote-controlled exhaust that shoots out flames.
Julien’s called it “one of the most recognised and important cinematic vehicles in Hollywood history.”
However, the new owner won’t be cruising the streets in it. The car is not street legal, which means it can’t be driven on public roads. It must also stay parked whenever it’s shown to the public.
The car has spent years on display at the Marconi Automotive Museum in California, and the auction takes place in Gardena on Tuesday.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/black-cap: The Black Caps battled through a windy final day at the Basin Reserve in Wellington to draw the first cricket Test against India on 23 November 2026.
India had scored 720 runs for nine wickets before declaring, which means choosing to stop batting. That gave them a huge lead of 352 runs.

To save the match, New Zealand had to bat for the whole day without losing all their wickets. They started at 119 for two and played so carefully that it took 18 balls to score their first run of the morning.

Devon Conway made 65 and Rachin Ravindra made 37 before both were out. Glenn Phillips, who scored a century in the first innings, made 26. He and Daryl Mitchell put on 63 runs together, and Mitchell finished not out on 49.
New Zealand were 239 for five when the captains shook hands to end the match. India were still five wickets short of a win.
In Test cricket, if time runs out before either team can win, the match is a draw.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/world-lea: Leaders and scientists from around the world have been meeting in Antalya, Turkey, for a huge United Nations climate conference called COP31 – but talks on an important part of the deal have hit a wall.

Climate scientist Dr Bill Hare, who helps write major international climate reports, said talks about climate finance – money that richer countries give to help poorer countries deal with climate change – are “totally blocked right now.”

“One of the biggest worries at this COP is that there has not been, essentially, the big plan about it,” he said. He wants wealthy countries to triple the money they give to help vulnerable nations adapt to a warmer world, such as by protecting homes from floods and storms.

Dr Hare also pointed out that a small number of countries have been blocking funding and cooperation for the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the group of scientists that reviews climate research for the whole world.

On a more positive note, Dr Hare welcomed strong wording in the draft agreement about moving away from fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas, towards cleaner energy. He said it might be tricky to keep that wording in the final agreement, but he hoped it would survive.
Talks at COP31 are expected to continue as leaders try to find common ground before the summit wraps up.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/fiji-clai: Fiji’s rugby team celebrated a big 21-16 win over Italy on Saturday, in a thrilling Nations Championship match played at Bluenergy Stadium in Udine, Italy.

The Flying Fijians fought hard for the win, scoring three tries to Italy’s one. Tevita Ikanivere crossed the line in the 44th minute, before Kitione Salawa added another try just seven minutes later to help seal the victory.

Italy actually held more of the ball during the match, with 54 percent possession compared to Fiji’s 46 percent. But Fiji’s defence was rock solid, making 167 tackles to Italy’s 135, showing just how hard the Pacific side worked without the ball.
Key Fijian players Josua Tuisova and Selestino Ravutaumada both caused problems for Italy’s defence throughout the game, helping Fiji control the biggest moments.
The win is a great result for Fiji as they continue to build their reputation on the world rugby stage, against tough European opposition on the road.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/rotorua-r: Rotorua runner Hannah Gapes has won the NCAA Division I women’s cross country championship in Terre Haute, Indiana, in the United States, and set a course record.
The NCAA runs university sport in the United States, and Division I is its top level. Cross country is running over grass, dirt and hills rather than on a track.

Gapes, who runs for North Carolina State University (NC State), finished the 6km course in 18 minutes 44.3 seconds on 21 November 2026 (US time). She crossed the line more than seven seconds ahead of second place, Salma Elbadra from South Carolina.
She is only the second New Zealander to win the women’s title. The first was Kim Smith, who won on the same course 22 years ago.
It was Gapes’ last ever NCAA cross country race, and it finished off an unbeaten season. She took 13 seconds off the course record she set there in October.
Gapes was also New Zealand’s women’s senior cross country champion in 2025.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/niue-ocea: A project protecting the ocean around the small Pacific nation of Niue has won one of the world’s most prestigious environmental prizes.

The Niue Ocean Wide Trust took out the Revive Our Oceans category at the Earthshot Prize, awarded at a ceremony in Mumbai, India. Nearly 7000 projects from 169 countries entered this year, so winning is a huge achievement.
Prince William and Princess Catherine attended the ceremony, along with former New Zealand Prime Minister Dame Jacinda Ardern and Niue’s Prime Minister, Dalton Tagelagi.

The prize is worth millions of dollars. The trust works in partnership with the Niue Government, and people and groups around the world can already sponsor the protection of one square kilometre of Niue’s ocean for NZ$250 each.

The money raised so far has helped fund coastal protection projects in local villages, paid for insurance in case of climate disasters like cyclones, and even helped pay for half of Niue’s high school students to learn how to scuba dive.
In a Facebook post, the trust said the win belonged to the people of Niue.
Niue is aiming to raise $32 million in total to protect and manage its huge ocean area. Winning the Earthshot Prize has now pushed them over the halfway mark towards that goal.
